lesson.title: A device that remembers
lesson.subtitle: How often to measure, why readings wobble, and keeping a log

video.title: A device that remembers
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — science teacher, the student's teacher (main character)
Ms Salma — maths teacher, the student's teacher (cameo)
Dr Farah — education lecturer, the student's teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor in the school garden at dawn, frowning at a laptop log that shows 85 °C beside cool, dewy tomato plants.
scenes.animation: The 85 flashes red; a tomato steams comically, then the steam vanishes.
scenes.narration: Our garden sensor once logged eighty-five degrees at six in the morning. The tomatoes would have cooked! It was a glitch: that sensor says eighty-five as it wakes up. Today: a device that remembers, and which readings to trust.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: a device that remembers, with a time and a unit on every reading.

scenes.visual: A small logger box on a classroom wall; a loop of four arrows turns round it.
scenes.animation: The loop turns once per beat: read, store, wait, repeat.
scenes.narration: A data logger is a sensor with a memory: it reads, stores, waits, and repeats. The big question is how often. Too rarely, and you miss what happens in between. Too often, and you fill the memory and drain the battery.

scenes.visual: Three devices side by side, each with a clock showing how often it reads: a rain gauge, a classroom thermometer, a smoke alarm.
scenes.animation: Each clock ticks at its own speed.
scenes.narration: The rule of thumb: read faster than the thing changes. A rain gauge, once a day. A classroom's temperature, every five or ten minutes. A smoke alarm, every few seconds, because a fire can't wait.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma beside a bean seedling in a cup, with a ruler stood next to it. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! You're logging how fast a bean plant grows. Once a day, or every minute?

scenes.visual: A neat table of one height a day beside a scroll of repeated numbers that runs off the screen.
scenes.animation: The scroll keeps unrolling while the table stays tidy.
scenes.narration: Once a day. A bean plant grows slowly, so a daily reading catches every change. Every minute gives over a thousand near-identical numbers a day.

scenes.visual: A thermometer's display flickers between three values while the room stays the same.
scenes.animation: Each value pops up in turn with a small shake.
scenes.on_screen_text: Every reading is a little wrong
scenes.narration: Surprise: every reading is a little wrong. Read the same room three times, and you might get twenty-nine and a half, thirty and a half, then thirty. That wobble is called noise, and cheap sensors have more of it.

scenes.visual: Three readings slide into a box marked average and come out as one steady number.
scenes.animation: The three numbers merge into 30; then a real rise reaches the average a moment late.
scenes.narration: To calm the noise, average the last few readings: add them up and divide. These three average exactly thirty, so one jumpy reading can't switch the fan on by mistake. But the average reacts later, because it remembers older readings.

scenes.visual: Three readings on a seesaw: two 30s and one heavy 85 that tips the average up; the middle one stays put.
scenes.animation: The 85 drops in and the average shoots up; the median marker doesn't move.
scenes.narration: Averaging has a weak spot. Mix our eighty-five degree glitch with two real readings of thirty, and the average jumps above forty-eight. The middle reading, the median, stays at thirty. So remove glitches first, and write down what you removed.

scenes.visual: One row of a log table fills in: time, reading, unit, place. Then the unit cell empties and question marks appear.
scenes.animation: Cells type in one by one; the unit cell blinks out.
scenes.narration: A memory is only useful if it makes sense later. So every reading gets a time, a unit and a place: Monday at ten fifteen, thirty degrees Celsius, the science room. Without a unit, thirty could mean anything.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah beside a gas alarm on a lab wall, a slow ten-minute timer beside it. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A gas alarm averages its last ten minutes of readings, to hide the noise. Good idea?

scenes.visual: Four cards line up: a clock, a wobbling needle, an average sign, a log row.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: No: a gas alarm must react at once. Remember: read as often as the job needs. Every reading wobbles; averaging calms it but reacts later. And give every reading a time, a unit and a place.

scenes.visual: A student in a school yard measuring a stick's shadow with a ruler, a notebook table beside them.
scenes.animation: The shadow shortens towards noon as rows fill the table.
scenes.narration: Try it this week: be a data logger for a day. Every hour, read a thermometer, or measure a stick's shadow in the sun. Write the time, the reading and the unit in a table, then look for the pattern.

checkpoints.prompt: You're logging how fast a bean plant grows. How often should you measure it?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a plant grows slowly, so one reading a day catches every change.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — every minute gives 1,440 almost identical readings a day and drains the battery. A plant grows slowly: once a day is enough.

checkpoints.prompt: A gas alarm averages its last 10 minutes of readings, to hide noise. Good idea?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a gas leak can't wait ten minutes. A fan can wait; a gas alarm must react at once.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — it would give fewer false alarms, but it would react minutes too late, and a gas leak can't wait.
